summary:
Bangladesh is a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The protests that forced Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina from office in August 2024 are the inflection point: hardline conservative Islamist groups gained ground in the aftermath, and trans people who had previously lived and worked openly were driven into hiding. A Washington Blade assessment published on 5 August 2025, a year after the ouster, found the country's LGBTQ community increasingly vulnerable to violence amid Islamist mobilisation and threats.

The legal baseline is hostile but inconsistently applied. Section 377 of the Penal Code 1860 criminalises intercourse against the order of nature with a penalty of up to life imprisonment. Prosecutions are rare, but Outright International reports that police use the provision to harass people presumed to be LGBTIQ. At the same time, hijra have been officially recognised as a third gender since 2014, gender-marker change is permitted, and hijra and LGBTIQ pride events have been held.

The current incident baseline is set by the advocacy group JMBF, whose annual report published in April 2026 records 260 human-rights violations affecting at least 426 LGBTQI+ individuals nationwide during 2025. JMBF describes this as a sharp increase continuing an upward trend dating from 2022. The violations include murder and attempted murder, assault, abduction, arbitrary arrest, fabricated charges and extortion.

Lethal violence against visible trans people continues. On 3 February 2025, the prominent trans advocate Shila, originally from Chattogram district, was murdered in her home in Betbunia, Rangamati district; five unidentified individuals were accused in the case. She was widely known for humanitarian work.

Extortion demands backed by police violence are a documented feature of daily exposure. After hijras refused to pay police extortion money on 10 September 2025, at least twelve were injured in a retaliatory attack at Gomdondi Phultala. On 17 September 2025, police arrested twelve hijras who were collecting money from vehicles carrying expatriates in Narayanganj, a traditional hijra livelihood.

Policing of visibly trans people reaches transport hubs. In April 2024, five transgender and hijra women were arrested while begging near Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka and received sentences of about a month in custody, according to JMBF.
tangentialFactors:
Formal legal recognition and lived security have moved in opposite directions. Bangladesh recognised third-gender identity officially in 2013, and in 2021 a rural town elected a trans woman as mayor; reporting by Global Press Journal records that the trans people featured in its coverage now live in hiding.

The scope of Section 377 remains contested. The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity for Bangladesh, issued in September 2023 and updated in April 2026, states that it remains unclear whether lesbianism falls within the provision. ILGA's 2019 State-Sponsored Homophobia report read female-female activity as not criminal while elsewhere describing the provision as relevant to all genders.

Asylum-grade country material documents state-tolerated hostility beyond individual incidents. A UK Upper Tribunal decision of February 2019 (PA/07096/2017), citing fact-finding missions and Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada material, records Islamist groups calling for LGBT people to be prosecuted under Section 377 and Sharia, threats against LGBT journalists, and a government that does not recognise LGBT issues.
localsOnly:
Hijra have been legally recognised as a third gender since 2014 and are permitted to change gender markers on official documents. Community visibility is nonetheless constrained: a well-known trans advocate was killed at her home in Rangamati district in February 2025, and trans people reported by international media since the 2024 political upheaval describe living in hiding.

Street-based income collection, including seeking money from passengers on expatriate-carrying vehicles, is a long-established hijra livelihood and is treated by police as grounds for arrest. Twelve hijras were arrested in Narayanganj in September 2025 on these grounds; a refusal to hand over extortion money to police in the same month was followed by an attack in which at least twelve hijras were injured.

Policing of hijra begging extends to major transport infrastructure. Five hijra women were arrested and sentenced to roughly a month in custody in April 2024 after begging near the international airport in the capital.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the current inventory addresses entry or visa screening for trans visitors, including whether immigration or customs processing involves questions or documentation checks that could disclose a person's trans status. This remains unresolved.

Whether the third-gender marker available to Bangladeshi citizens under domestic law can be reflected on documents presented at the border by foreign visitors is not sourced here and is unresolved.

The frequency with which Section 377 is actually prosecuted against individuals rather than invoked as a harassment tool is described only in general terms by Outright International; the current inventory contains no court-level data, and this remains unresolved.

The April 2026 JMBF figures are compiled by an advocacy organisation and have not been cross-checked in the inventory against police or prosecutorial statistics.
